title: Idempotency Keys
one_liner: The client picks a unique key so a retried request runs at most once.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** The caller generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it with the request. The server stores the key alongside the result of the first execution. A second request carrying the same key does not re-execute: it returns the stored response. The key must be recorded in the *same transaction* as the side effect, or a crash between the two leaves you with a charge and no key.

**Where it bites.** Networks fail in the one place that matters: after the server committed but before the client saw the response. The client cannot distinguish "never arrived" from "arrived and succeeded", so it retries, and the user is charged twice. Idempotency moves the decision to the server, which is the only party that knows.

**The hard parts.** Key scope (per user? per endpoint?), retention (Stripe keeps keys 24 hours), and what to do when the same key arrives with a *different* body — that is a client bug, and returning the original result silently hides it. Return a 422 instead.

**Takeaway.** Any endpoint that moves money, sends a message, or creates a resource needs this. "The client will only call it once" is not a design.

title: CAP, In Practice
one_liner: You do not choose between C and A; you choose what to do during a partition.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** CAP says that when the network partitions, a replicated system must either refuse to answer (preserving consistency) or answer from possibly-stale state (preserving availability). It is a statement about a specific failure mode, not a ranking of databases.

**Why the popular version is wrong.** "We picked AP" is usually meaningless, because partitions are rare and the interesting tradeoff is the one you make *all the time*: latency versus staleness. That is PACELC — **P**artition: **A** or **C**, **E**lse **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Most systems that call themselves AP are really choosing L over C on every single read, partition or not.

**Where it bites.** Teams read CAP as permission to skip reasoning about consistency entirely. Then a user updates their profile, a read hits a lagging replica, the UI shows the old value, and the user clicks save again on stale data. No partition occurred; the problem was replica lag, which CAP never mentioned.

**Takeaway.** Ask the real question: what does a read return when the last write went to another replica, and what does the user do with that answer?

title: Read-Your-Writes Consistency
one_liner: The weakest guarantee that stops a user seeing their own edit vanish.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** After a session performs a write, every subsequent read *in that session* must reflect it. Other sessions may still see the old value. This is a session guarantee, not a global one, which is what makes it cheap.

**How it is implemented.** Three common ways: route the session to the primary for a short window after a write; have the write return a log position (an LSN, a timestamp, a token) and require later reads to wait until the replica has caught up to it; or read from the primary for just the records the session touched.

**Where it bites.** The classic bug: user edits their avatar, the write goes to the primary, the page reloads, the read hits a replica 200ms behind, and the old avatar appears. The user concludes the save failed. Note that caching makes this worse, because a CDN or an application cache can hold the stale value far longer than replication lag.

**Takeaway.** Pure eventual consistency is almost never acceptable for a user's view of their own data. Read-your-writes is the floor, and it is usually one token away.

title: LSM Trees
one_liner: Trade read amplification for write throughput by never updating in place.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Writes go to an in-memory table (the memtable) plus a write-ahead log, and nothing else. When the memtable fills, it is flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file (an SSTable). Reads check the memtable, then each level of SSTables, newest first. Background compaction merges SSTables to bound how many a read must consult and to discard overwritten keys.

**Why it is fast to write.** Every write is sequential. A B-tree, by contrast, must find and modify the right page, which is a random write, and it writes a whole page to change one row. LSM trees turn random writes into sequential ones at the cost of making reads check several places.

**The three amplifications.** *Write* amplification: compaction rewrites the same data repeatedly. *Read* amplification: one logical read touches many files (mitigated with bloom filters per SSTable). *Space* amplification: obsolete versions live until compaction. Leveled compaction minimises space and read amplification; size-tiered minimises write amplification. You cannot minimise all three — that is the RUM conjecture.

**Where you meet them.** RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, and the storage engines under ClickHouse and InfluxDB.

**Takeaway.** If your workload is write-heavy with range scans, this is the shape. If it is read-heavy point lookups on a small dataset, a B-tree still wins.

title: MVCC
one_liner: Readers never block writers because each sees its own snapshot of history.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Instead of overwriting a row, the database writes a new version of it, tagged with the transaction that created it. Every transaction gets a snapshot — a rule for which versions are visible to it. A reader walks the version chain and picks the newest version visible under its snapshot. Writers append; they do not block readers, and readers do not block writers.

**The cost nobody plans for.** Old versions must be collected. In PostgreSQL that is `VACUUM`, and a long-running transaction pins every version created since it started, because that transaction might still need to see them. One forgotten `BEGIN` in a psql session can bloat a table by gigabytes and make the planner's statistics useless. In MySQL/InnoDB the same problem appears as a growing undo log and "history list length".

**Snapshot isolation is not serializable.** Two transactions can each read a consistent snapshot, each write a disjoint row, and together break an invariant neither broke alone — write skew. The textbook case is two doctors both dropping their on-call shift because each sees the other still on call. Fix it with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, a serializable isolation level, or a constraint the database can check.

**Takeaway.** MVCC is why your reads are fast and why your table is 40GB for 2GB of rows.

links.title: A critique of ANSI SQL isolation levels

title: Write Skew
one_liner: Two transactions that are individually correct can break an invariant together.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Under snapshot isolation, each transaction reads a consistent snapshot and writes rows no one else wrote. No write-write conflict occurs, so both commit. But each made its decision based on rows the *other* then changed. The invariant spanned both row sets, and nothing checked it.

**The canonical example.** Hospital rule: at least one doctor on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. Each opens a transaction, reads "two doctors on call, fine", and takes themselves off. Both commit. Zero doctors on call. Neither transaction wrote a row the other read-locked, because snapshot isolation locks nothing on read.

**Recognising it in your own code.** Look for: read a set of rows, make a decision from an aggregate over them, then write. Booking the last seat, enforcing a unique username without a unique index, enforcing a balance floor across several accounts, claiming a job from a queue.

**The fixes, in order of preference.** A database constraint (unique index, check, exclusion constraint) — the database checks it for you. Then `SERIALIZABLE` isolation (PostgreSQL's SSI will abort one transaction; you must retry). Then materialising the conflict: lock an explicit row that represents the invariant, so the two transactions do conflict.

**Takeaway.** "We use transactions" does not mean "our invariants hold". Isolation level is part of the invariant.

title: Index Selectivity
one_liner: An index helps only when it eliminates most of the table.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Selectivity is the fraction of rows a predicate keeps. An index lookup costs a tree descent plus, for a non-covering index, one random read per matching row to fetch the rest of the row. A sequential scan reads every page but does so sequentially. Past roughly 5–10% of the table, the random reads lose and the planner switches to a scan. This is why your index on `status` (three distinct values) is never used, and why you concluded "the planner is broken".

**Composite index order.** With an index on `(a, b)`, a query on `a` alone works, a query on `b` alone does not. The rule is leftmost prefix. Put equality columns first, then the range column, then columns you only need for output. A sort can also be served by the index if its order matches `ORDER BY`.

**Covering indexes.** If the index contains every column the query touches (`INCLUDE` in PostgreSQL, a secondary index with the columns in MySQL), the heap fetch disappears and the random-read cost goes away. That can move the crossover point substantially.

**What to actually do.** Read `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`. Compare the planner's row estimate with the real count. A 100x misestimate means stale statistics, a correlated predicate the planner assumes is independent, or a function wrapping the column so the index cannot be used at all.

**Takeaway.** Indexes are not a performance setting you turn on. Each one is a bet about selectivity, and you can read whether the bet paid off.

title: Connection Pooling and Pool Exhaustion
one_liner: A Postgres connection is a process; the pool is the real concurrency limit.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Each PostgreSQL connection is an OS process with its own memory (`work_mem` is per operation, per connection). A few hundred of them will exhaust a server that handles thousands of queries per second happily on twenty. So you put a pool in front: application-side (HikariCP, `pg.Pool`, SQLAlchemy) or a proxy (PgBouncer, pgcat, RDS Proxy).

**The counterintuitive result.** Throughput peaks at a *small* pool. The useful rule of thumb is roughly `cores * 2 + effective_spindle_count`. Beyond that, connections queue inside the database instead of outside it, context switching and lock contention rise, and p99 gets worse while the dashboard still shows idle CPU.

**Pool exhaustion.** The failure looks like a hang, not an error: every connection is checked out, and new requests block on acquisition until they time out. Three usual causes — a transaction left open across an HTTP call or a slow external API; a leaked connection on an error path that never returns it; and N+1 queries multiplying hold time. Always set an acquisition timeout, or a slow database becomes an unavailable application.

**Transaction vs session pooling.** PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes connections per transaction, which is far more efficient but breaks anything relying on session state: prepared statements, `SET`, advisory locks, `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, temp tables.

**Takeaway.** Your concurrency limit is the pool size, whether you chose it or not. Pick it deliberately and set a timeout on acquisition.

title: Backpressure
one_liner: A queue that cannot say no is a queue that will fall over.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Backpressure is the signal a slow consumer sends upstream to make a fast producer slow down. Without it, the mismatch accumulates somewhere: an unbounded queue, a growing heap, a socket buffer, a disk. The system does not reject work; it accepts work it will never finish, and then dies with everything in flight.

**Unbounded queues are the anti-pattern.** An unbounded queue converts an overload problem into a latency problem and then into an out-of-memory crash. Bound every queue. Once bounded, you must decide what happens when it is full, and that decision is the design: block the producer (propagates backpressure naturally), drop the newest, drop the oldest (often right for telemetry — fresh data beats stale), or reject with a 429 and a `Retry-After`.

**Why latency is the wrong signal to monitor.** Under overload, latency rises before throughput falls, so a queue that is already doomed looks merely slow. Watch queue *depth* and *wait time*, and the ratio of arrival rate to service rate. Little's Law (`L = λW`) tells you the rest.

**Load shedding beats queuing.** A request whose client has already timed out is pure waste — you pay to compute a response nobody reads. Check the deadline before starting work, and drop requests that cannot finish in time. This is the single highest-leverage overload defence in most services.

**Takeaway.** Every link in the chain needs a bound and a documented behaviour at that bound. "It scales" means "it degrades predictably".

title: Circuit Breaker
one_liner: Stop calling a dependency that is already failing, so you fail fast instead of piling up.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A breaker wraps a remote call and tracks its failure rate. In `closed` state, calls pass through. When failures cross a threshold, it trips to `open` and fails immediately without calling — no socket, no timeout wait. After a cooldown it moves to `half-open` and lets a few probes through; success closes it, failure re-opens it.

**The problem it actually solves.** It is not about the failing dependency; it is about *you*. Without a breaker, every request to the sick service occupies a thread or a connection for the full timeout. Those resources are shared, so your healthy endpoints starve and a single slow dependency takes the whole service down. That is the cascading failure.

**Getting it wrong.** Too sensitive and you trip on normal jitter, turning a 1% error rate into a 100% outage. Thresholds should be a *rate over a window* with a minimum request count, never a raw count. And the breaker needs a fallback: a cached value, a degraded response, a queued retry. A breaker without a fallback just converts slow failures into fast ones, which is an improvement but not a feature.

**Related tools.** Bulkheads (separate pools per dependency, so one cannot starve the others) and timeouts (a breaker cannot help if your timeout is 60 seconds, because you will exhaust the pool long before the threshold trips). Timeouts first, then bulkheads, then breakers.

**Takeaway.** Set the timeout, isolate the pool, then add the breaker. In that order.

title: Exponential Backoff with Jitter
one_liner: Retries without jitter re-synchronise your clients into a self-inflicted DDoS.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** On failure, wait `base * 2^attempt` before retrying, capped at some maximum, then add randomness. The exponential part gives an overloaded dependency room to recover. The random part — jitter — is the half everyone skips, and it is the half that matters.

**Why jitter is not optional.** A dependency blips and fails a thousand requests at once. Every client computes the same backoff and retries at the same instant. The dependency, still recovering, falls over again. The clients retry again, still in lockstep. You have built a retry storm, and it is periodic. Jitter spreads the herd out.

**Which jitter.** AWS measured the variants: *full jitter* (`sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^n))`) wins on both completion time and total work in most cases. "Equal jitter" (half fixed, half random) is marginally more predictable. Decorrelated jitter is competitive. Plain exponential with no jitter is always worst.

**The parts that are not the sleep.** Only retry idempotent operations, or carry an idempotency key. Cap *total* attempts and total elapsed time, not just the interval. Never retry a 4xx — the request is wrong, and retrying it is pure load. Use a retry budget: a token bucket that caps retries at, say, 10% of normal traffic, so a widespread failure cannot multiply your load. And do not retry at every layer: three layers each retrying three times is twenty-seven requests.

**Takeaway.** `retry(3)` with no jitter, no budget and no idempotency is how a brief blip becomes an outage.

links.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library)

title: Thundering Herd and Cache Stampede
one_liner: One expired key, a thousand simultaneous recomputations.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A hot cache key expires. Every concurrent request misses, and every one of them starts the expensive recomputation — the same query, the same render, the same fan-out. The origin receives a load spike proportional to your traffic, which is exactly when you can least afford it. Worse, the slow origin makes requests pile up, so the herd grows while it waits.

**Three fixes, composable.** *Locking / request coalescing*: the first miss takes a lock and computes; the others wait for its result or serve stale. Go's `singleflight` and Nginx's `proxy_cache_lock` are this. *Stale-while-revalidate*: serve the expired value immediately and refresh in the background, so no user ever waits for a recompute. *Probabilistic early expiry*: each reader independently decides to refresh with a probability that rises as the TTL approaches, so refreshes spread out instead of landing together.

**TTL jitter.** If you populate ten thousand keys in one deploy with identical TTLs, they expire together. Randomise TTLs by ±10% and the cliff becomes a slope.

**Beyond caches.** The same shape appears in cron jobs that all fire at `0 * * * *`, clients that reconnect simultaneously after a deploy, and token refreshes that all expire at once. Any synchronised schedule is a herd waiting to happen.

**Takeaway.** Caches turn load problems into coordination problems. Coalesce, serve stale, and jitter your TTLs.

title: Bloom Filters
one_liner: A few kilobytes that tell you, with no false negatives, what is definitely absent.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A bit array of size `m` and `k` independent hash functions. To insert, hash the element `k` times and set those bits. To query, hash and check: if any bit is 0 the element is *definitely absent*; if all are 1 it is *probably present*. No false negatives, tunable false positives, no deletions, and no way to enumerate what is in it.

**The numbers worth memorising.** About 10 bits per element gives a 1% false positive rate; 14 bits gives 0.1%. That is independent of element size — a million 200-byte URLs fit in roughly 1.2MB at 1%, versus ~200MB for a hash set. The optimal `k` is `(m/n) * ln2`, around 7 for the 1% case.

**Where it earns its place.** Every SSTable in an LSM tree carries one, so a point lookup skips files that cannot contain the key — that is what makes LSM reads tolerable. CDNs use them to decide whether an object is worth caching on first request. Chrome shipped one for malicious URLs. Bitcoin used them for light-client filtering.

**Know the variants.** *Counting* Bloom filters support deletion at 3–4x the space. *Cuckoo* filters support deletion and beat Bloom on space below ~3% error. *Quotient* filters are more cache-friendly. If you need counts rather than membership, you want Count-Min Sketch; if you need cardinality, HyperLogLog.

**Takeaway.** When a "probably" is cheap and a "definitely not" is valuable, this is the structure. Always ask what a false positive costs you before you reach for it.

title: Consistent Hashing
one_liner: Adding a node should move 1/n of the keys, not all of them.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** `hash(key) % n` is catastrophic under resizing: change `n` and almost every key maps somewhere new, so every cache misses and every shard rebalances at once. Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a ring. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. Add or remove a node and only the keys between it and its predecessor move — about `1/n` of them.

**Virtual nodes.** With one point per node, the ring is lumpy: some nodes own far more of the keyspace than others, and removing a node dumps all its load onto a single neighbour. Give each physical node 100–200 virtual points and the distribution smooths out and the load of a departing node spreads across all the others. Every real implementation does this.

**Bounded loads.** Even with virtual nodes, a hot key or a skewed workload can overload one node. Consistent hashing *with bounded loads* caps any node at `(1+ε)` times the average, spilling to the next node on the ring when it is full. Useful for request routing, not for storage placement.

**The alternatives.** Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing is simpler — hash `(key, node)` for every node and take the max — and gives perfect distribution with no virtual nodes, at `O(n)` per lookup. Jump consistent hash is faster and smaller still, but cannot handle arbitrary node removal, only shrinking the tail.

**Where you will meet it.** Memcached clients, Cassandra and DynamoDB partitioning, Envoy's ring-hash load balancer, and any sharded cache you are about to resize.

title: Raft
one_liner: Consensus you can actually hold in your head: one leader, an append-only log, a majority.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** Raft decomposes consensus into three problems. *Leader election*: nodes are followers until one times out, becomes a candidate, and wins a majority vote for a numbered term. *Log replication*: all writes go to the leader, which appends them and replicates to followers; an entry commits once a majority have it. *Safety*: a candidate can only win if its log is at least as up to date as the majority's, which guarantees a new leader never discards committed entries.

**Why it exists.** Paxos is correct and famously hard to implement correctly. Raft was explicitly designed for understandability — strong leadership, no holes in the log, and terms as a logical clock — and it won: etcd, Consul, TiKV, CockroachDB, RabbitMQ quorum queues, Kafka's KRaft and Redpanda all run Raft or a close variant.

**What it costs you.** Every write is a majority round trip, so write latency is bounded below by your slowest-of-majority network hop — which is why a three-region Raft group has a floor of tens of milliseconds per write. Throughput is bounded by the leader. A majority must be alive: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. An even number of nodes buys you nothing.

**The parts that bite in production.** Reading from the leader is not automatically linearizable — a deposed leader may not know it yet, so you need a lease or a read index. Membership changes are a protocol step, not a config edit. And a slow follower can silently become a liability long before it is "down".

**Takeaway.** Raft gives you a replicated log. Everything else — a KV store, a lock service, a state machine — is what you build on top of it.

links.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm

title: Vector Clocks and Logical Time
one_liner: Wall clocks cannot order events across machines; counters can.
body_md:
**The mechanism.** A Lamport clock is a counter per node: increment on every local event, and on receiving a message set your counter to `max(local, received) + 1`. This guarantees that if A caused B then `time(A) < time(B)`. It does *not* tell you the converse, so you cannot distinguish concurrency from causality. A vector clock fixes that: each node keeps a vector of counters, one per node. Compare two vectors element-wise — if every element of A is ≤ B, A happened before B; if neither dominates, the events are genuinely concurrent.

**What that buys you.** Concurrency becomes detectable rather than silently resolved. Dynamo used vector clocks so a conflicting write surfaced as *siblings* the application could merge, instead of last-write-wins quietly deleting a user's shopping cart item. Git's commit graph is the same idea made concrete: parents encode causality, and a merge is how you resolve a concurrent pair.

**Why wall clocks fail.** NTP drift, leap seconds, VM pauses and clock skew between machines are all larger than the intervals you are trying to order. "Last write wins by timestamp" means "whichever machine's clock is fastest wins", which is a data-loss policy, not a conflict-resolution policy. Google's TrueTime and Spanner's commit-wait exist precisely because getting ordering from physical clocks requires bounding the uncertainty in hardware.

**The cost.** Vectors grow with the number of writers, so long-lived objects accumulate entries. Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) are the common compromise: a physical timestamp plus a logical counter, so values are human-readable, close to real time, and still respect causality.

**Takeaway.** If two replicas disagree, the question is never "which is newer" but "are these concurrent". Only logical time can answer it.
